conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're here because your blood sugar was extremely high and you’ve been feeling unwell. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been really anxious lately. My sugars were in the 200s this morning, but then they jumped to over 600. I’ve been thirsty, peeing a lot, and I’ve thrown up a few times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. We also saw you had some rectal bleeding in the ER. Did you notice that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I did have a few loose stools, but I didn’t see blood. I’ve had stomach issues before with my diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we know you have a history of gastroparesis. Right now, your labs show diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. That means your body is producing too many ketones because it doesn’t have enough insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I missed a few insulin doses. I was so nauseous I didn’t eat, so I thought I didn’t need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common mistake, but even when you’re not eating, your body still needs insulin. We’re starting an insulin drip to bring your levels down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been so dizzy and thirsty. Is that from the DKA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. DKA causes dehydration and high blood sugar, which leads to thirst, frequent urination, and nausea. We’re giving you IV fluids to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My back’s been hurting too. I usually take oxycodone, but I didn’t want to mix it with everything else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage your pain with safer options like Tylenol and ibuprofen. We’re avoiding narcotics unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar has come down to 280, and your ketones are improving. We’re transitioning you from the insulin drip to subcutaneous insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I haven’t vomited since last night. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on a diabetic diet. Small, frequent meals are best. We’re also checking your thiamine levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thiamine? Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because people with poor nutrition and chronic illness, especially with vomiting, can become deficient. We found yours was low, so we’re starting supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I haven’t been eating much. Thank you for catching that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray yesterday. It showed a lack of bowel gas, which is common in gastroparesis. No blockage, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel so full and nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your stomach is emptying slowly. That’s why we’re holding off on metoclopramide for now — we want to see if your DKA improvement helps your stomach function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. My anxiety’s been worse too. I’ve been on sertraline, but it doesn’t feel like it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry reviewed your case. They recommend increasing your sertraline to 100 mg daily. We’ll also keep your lorazepam for breakthrough anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try that. I just don’t want to keep ending up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting you up with endocrinology and your psychiatrist after discharge. But we also need you to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but I’ve been overwhelmed. I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar spiked again last night, and your acid levels started to rise. We had to restart the insulin drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so frustrated. I thought I was getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s okay. This is common in DKA recovery. We’re adjusting your insulin regimen. We’ll try glargine at night and a sliding scale for meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me avoid the ICU again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. We’re also adding dextrose to your IV to prevent low blood sugar while you’re not eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your DKA has resolved. Your last blood sugar was 150, and you’ve kept down breakfast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s a relief. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to make sure your sugars stay stable. We’re increasing your glargine to 25 units at night to see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’ve had lows before with higher doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. If you have morning lows, we’ll lower it back. Safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had to lower your glargine back to 20 units. You had a fasting glucose of 60 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt shaky. I’m glad you caught it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it at 20 units. If your morning sugars are over 140, you can increase by 2 units every two days until they improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll write that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also starting lidocaine patches for your back pain. They’re safer than narcotics long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve used them before. They help. Can I also take ibuprofen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, up to 400 mg every 8 hours as needed. Just not on an empty stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. No infection was found — blood and urine cultures were clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all goes well. You’ll follow up with GI for your nausea and your psychiatrist for your anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment with my psychiatrist already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s scheduled. And endocrinology wants you to call them to set up a visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. I know I need to take better care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line today so you can get IV fluids at home if needed, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that necessary? I’m feeling much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a precaution. If you can’t keep fluids down again, you can get treated at home instead of coming back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line was placed successfully. You’re doing well. We’ll remove the IV and prepare for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can you go over my new medications again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’ll take 20 units of glargine at bedtime. Increase by 2 units every two days if your morning sugar is over 140.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fast-acting insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your aspart per the sliding scale based on your fingerstick. Stop the metoclopramide. Take sertraline 100 mg daily, thiamine 100 mg daily, and use the lidocaine patch as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No more reglan. I’ll take notes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re doing well — alert, eating, and your sugars are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I’ll try to follow up and take better care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Call your doctors, check your sugars regularly, and don’t skip insulin — even if you’re not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise. I don’t want to be back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all instructions and prescriptions with you. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.
